item.description:

Why did closely related North Germanic varieties undergo different trajectories during the medieval long back vowel shift (Stora Vokaldansen)? While Swedish and much of Norwegian underwent successive raising of /ɑː/, /oː/, and /uː/, Danish underwent only the initial rounding of /ɑː/ to /ɔː/. It has long been known that there is much dialectal variation among tense forms in English irregular verbs, particularly among the simple past and past participle forms. Such variation has often been analysed as analogical levelling, whereby the past participle usually levels towards the simple past forms (e.g., I spoke/have spoke). item.dc:creator: Radim Lacina
Utku Turk
item.description:
Radim Lacina; Utku Turk · PsyArXiv + LingBuzz

This is a review of Dan Parker's book 'Linguistic illusions: A case study on agreement attraction' published by Cambridge University Press in 2025. The book gives a comprehensive summary of both the basics of a myriad of illusory phenomena and of agreement attraction in detail. It is a valuable resource for students and researchers alike, especially thanks to the accessible explanations of the leading issues and theories in the field. We critically discuss the book's reported ACT-R modelling, original experiments and its limited engagement with the cross-linguistic study of attraction.

We argue that the Micro-cue Model is perfect for capturing this variation, as it assumes that the different instantiations of verb placement and residual V2 in English are acquired separately.

item.title: An exoskeletal grammar approach to linguistic flexibility
item.dc:creator: Tor A. Åfarli
item.description:
Tor A. Åfarli · Zenodo

This paper shows how a simple and robust version of an exoskeletal grammar model (dubbed the Exoskeletal Frame Model) is able to account for two ubiquitous types of linguistic flexibility, namely argument structure flexibility and lexical creativity. In both areas, it is concluded that an exoskeletal model should be preferred to a traditional lexicalist or endoskeletal model. The tenor of the paper is somewhat programmatic, seeking to make clear the principled differences between endoskeletalism on the one hand and exoskeletalism on the other, and simultaneously trying to point out the essential motivation for adopting the exoskeletal approach.

This volume explores issues relating to language variation, acquisition, and change. It consists of 27 chapters that illuminate these issues from a range of different methodological, empirical, and theoretical perspectives. Many chapters also combine two or even three of the themes, illustrating that they are linked and that such combinations increase our understanding of a particular phenomenon.
